content:
Quick answer: Your GP or another clinician refers you to the service you need, such as rheumatology, orthopaedics or community MSK physiotherapy. In England most referrals go through the NHS e-Referral Service, you can usually choose your hospital, and your 18-week clock starts when the referral is received. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently, even if blood tests are normal.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS Choice Framework, the NHS guide to waiting times in England, NHS England information on Advice and Guidance, NHS Digital's e-Referral Service, NHS inform, GOV.WALES, Northern Ireland Department of Health statistics and NICE guidelines.

A referral is how one part of the NHS asks another to see you. For arthritis, that might be your GP referring you to rheumatology, a physiotherapist referring you to orthopaedics, or you referring yourself to community physiotherapy. Understanding how referrals work helps you check yours is on track, make choices, and know what to do if it seems to have stalled.

Who can refer you

  • Your GP, the most common route to hospital specialists such as rheumatology and orthopaedics.
  • Other primary care professionals, such as first contact physiotherapists in GP surgeries, advanced nurse practitioners and pharmacists, depending on local arrangements.
  • Community musculoskeletal (MSK) services, which may refer you on to hospital specialists.
  • Hospital specialists, who may refer you to another specialty or to therapy services.
  • Yourself. The NHS says that in many areas you can refer yourself to NHS community MSK physiotherapy without seeing a GP. Self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies is also available in England.

How a typical referral works in England

  1. Assessment. Your GP or another clinician assesses you and decides whether you need a referral, and how urgently.
  2. Advice before referral (sometimes). NHS England explains that GPs can use Advice and Guidance to ask a specialist for advice before, or instead of, referring you. This might lead to a test, a change in treatment, or advice about which service is most appropriate.
  3. Choice. For a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service, you usually have the legal right to choose the provider and the consultant-led team. Tell your clinician your preferences, as they choose the shortlist.
  4. The referral is sent. Most referrals in England go through the NHS e-Referral Service (e-RS), a digital platform used to refer patients and book appointments or send referrals for triage.
  5. Booking or triage. You may book the appointment yourself using the details in your appointment request letter, or the service may triage your referral first and contact you.
  6. The clock starts. The NHS says your waiting time starts when the hospital or service receives your referral letter, or when you book your first appointment through e-RS.
  7. First appointment. You are seen, assessed and may have tests. Your waiting-time clock keeps running while tests are done, until treatment starts or a decision is made that treatment is not needed.

Urgent and routine referrals

Referrals are prioritised by clinical need. For arthritis, the most important urgent route is for suspected inflammatory arthritis:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and similar conditions. NICE recommends referring any adult with suspected persistent synovitis (joint inflammation) of undetermined cause for a specialist opinion, and referring urgently if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or longer since symptoms started. This applies even if blood tests are normal. NICE's quality standard says this referral should happen within 3 working days of seeing a primary care clinician.
  • Suspected new inflammatory arthritis and spondyloarthritis. NICE recommends urgent referral to rheumatology for suspected new-onset inflammatory arthritis, and sets out criteria for referring people with long-term back pain that started before age 45 for a spondyloarthritis assessment.
  • Suspected temporal (giant cell) arteritis, with severe headaches, tenderness at the temples or scalp, jaw pain when eating or vision problems. The NHS says this needs urgent treatment because it can lead to stroke or blindness.
  • Osteoarthritis and most mechanical joint pain are usually routine referrals, often to community MSK services first.

If you think your referral should be urgent, say why: for example, "my finger joints are swollen and I have been stiff for over an hour every morning for six weeks."

Community MSK and triage services

In many areas, referrals for joint, back and muscle problems go first to a community MSK service, sometimes called an interface or triage service. These are often staffed by advanced practice physiotherapists, GPs with a special interest and other specialists. NICE's back pain guideline refers to musculoskeletal interface clinics as a specialist setting.

These services may:

  • assess and treat you directly, for example with physiotherapy, exercise programmes or injections
  • arrange tests such as X-rays, MRI or blood tests
  • refer you on to orthopaedics, rheumatology or a pain service if needed

Being seen in a community service is not a sign that your problem is not being taken seriously. It often means faster access to the right treatment. Ask how and when you would be referred on if needed.

Your right to choose (England)

The NHS Choice Framework explains that when you are referred for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service, you can usually choose:

  • which provider you go to, including many independent hospitals that hold NHS contracts
  • which consultant-led team you see

These choices apply at the point of referral, and normally the same provider goes on to provide the rest of your treatment. They do not apply in some situations, such as if you need urgent or emergency care, are in prison or are a serving member of the armed forces.

If you are likely to wait more than 18 weeks for non-urgent consultant-led treatment, you can ask to change provider. Contact the service treating you or your integrated care board (ICB). If you were not offered a choice, speak to the person who referred you first, then your ICB.

How to check your referral is on track

  • Ask at the time: Which service am I being referred to? Is it urgent or routine? When will it be sent? How will I hear?
  • Look out for a letter, text or email with booking details or confirmation that your referral has been received.
  • If you have an appointment request letter, use the details to book or check your appointment online or by phone.
  • If you hear nothing after a few weeks, contact your GP surgery to confirm the referral was sent, then contact the hospital or service's booking team.
  • Keep a note of the date of referral, the service and any reference numbers.

If your referral is returned or redirected

Sometimes a specialist service returns a referral with advice, or redirects it to a different service, such as community MSK or physiotherapy, because they think that is the most appropriate place to be seen. If this happens:

  • ask your GP what the specialist advised and why
  • check whether you have been referred somewhere else instead
  • if your symptoms are getting worse or have changed, ask your GP to send an updated referral with the new information

What goes in a referral letter

A good referral gives the specialist enough information to prioritise you correctly. It usually includes:

  • your symptoms, how long you have had them and how they are changing
  • examination findings, such as which joints are swollen
  • relevant test results, such as blood tests or X-rays
  • your other health conditions and medicines
  • what has already been tried, and whether it helped
  • how the problem affects your daily life and work
  • the question the referrer wants answered, for example "Is this inflammatory arthritis?" or "Would this patient benefit from joint replacement?"

Specialist teams often triage referrals on paper. If something important is missing, such as swollen joints or a rapidly worsening problem, your referral may be given a lower priority than it needs.

If you move house or change GP while waiting

Tell both your old and new GP surgery, and the hospital, as soon as you know your new address. If you can still travel to the same hospital, ask whether you can stay on its list. If not, ask whether your referral can be transferred to a hospital near your new home and how your waiting time will be treated. If you move between the UK nations, different waiting time rules apply, and you may need a new referral to services in your new area. Keep a record of your original referral date in case you need it.

How referrals differ across the UK

NationKey points
EnglandMost referrals via the NHS e-Referral Service. Legal right to choose provider for first consultant-led outpatient appointment, and right to start treatment within 18 weeks, with exceptions.
ScotlandReferral to your NHS health board's services. Standards of 12 weeks for a new outpatient appointment from receipt of referral and 18 weeks from referral to treatment, plus the legal 12-week Treatment Time Guarantee for planned inpatient and day-case treatment once agreed. No equivalent of England's legal right to choose any provider.
WalesReferral to your local health board. The Welsh Government's referral-to-treatment target is 26 weeks from receipt of referral for 95% of patients, with a maximum of 36 weeks, although these targets are not currently being met.
Northern IrelandReferral to your Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust. Some referrals go first to integrated clinical assessment and treatment services (ICATS). Referrals are prioritised as red flag, urgent or routine, and average waits are published on My Waiting Times NI.

See our waiting list guide for more on each nation's rules, and NHS arthritis pathways simplified for where a referral fits in the bigger picture.

Tips to make your referral as strong as possible

  • Describe the impact. Tell your GP what you cannot do, not just where it hurts. The referral letter should reflect how arthritis affects your work, sleep and daily life.
  • Bring a symptom record. Note which joints swell, how long morning stiffness lasts and what you have tried.
  • Mention related conditions, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or eye inflammation, which make inflammatory arthritis more likely.
  • Ask for a copy of the referral letter if you would like one, so you can check it is accurate.
  • Prepare for the appointment. See what happens at a rheumatology appointment.

Private referrals

If you choose to pay privately, you may need a referral letter from your GP or another clinician, depending on the provider. If you later want NHS treatment, your private consultant can write to your GP, who can refer you into the NHS. You may then be placed on the NHS waiting list according to clinical need. Read our guide to private treatment costs first.

When to get medical help

Do not wait for a referral to come through if you have:

  • a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever. Get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111
  • severe headaches, tenderness at your temples or scalp, jaw pain when eating, or vision problems. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, as this could be temporal arteritis
  • back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, or new problems controlling your bladder or bowels. Go to A&E or call 999
  • rapidly worsening symptoms, such as more joints swelling week by week. Contact your GP, who can update or upgrade the referral

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take for a GP referral to be received?

It varies. Many referrals are sent electronically. If you have not heard anything within a few weeks, check with your GP surgery that it was sent, then contact the hospital booking team.

When does my 18-week wait start?

In England, from when the hospital or service receives your referral, or when you book your first appointment through the NHS e-Referral Service.

Can I choose which hospital I am referred to?

In England, usually yes, for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not have the same legal right to choose.

Can I refer myself to a rheumatologist?

Not usually on the NHS. You can refer yourself to community MSK physiotherapy in many areas, but rheumatology referrals normally come from a GP or another clinician.

What is Advice and Guidance?

It is a way for your GP to ask a specialist for advice before or instead of referring you. It can lead to faster changes in treatment or a referral to the most suitable service.

My referral was sent back. What does that mean?

The specialist may have given advice to your GP, or redirected you to another service such as community MSK. Ask your GP what was advised and what happens next.
